analysis.one_liner: Cuts the legal arsenic limit in drinking water from 50 to 3 parts per billion and funds small water systems' upgrades.
analysis.headline: Despite 77 cosponsors, the bill never received a committee vote and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the Safe Drinking Water Act to lower the legal limit for arsenic in tap water from 50 parts per billion — a standard dating to 1942 — to 10 parts per billion by October 2003 and 3 parts per billion by October 2006. It also authorized $800 million a year in grants to help small public water systems, which make up 94% of all systems, pay for the required treatment. The bill cites a National Academy of Sciences study linking arsenic at the old standard to bladder, lung, and skin cancer. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to a subcommittee, and no vote was ever taken before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: The main beneficiaries would be the more than 34 million Americans the bill says drink water from systems with arsenic levels posing unacceptable cancer risks, who would get a much stricter legal limit on a known carcinogen [S3]. Small and rural communities would also benefit directly: the bill directs federal grants to water systems serving fewer than 10,000 people, sparing ratepayers in those towns the full cost of treatment upgrades, which is the reason small-town officials typically fight such mandates [S2] [S3]. Water treatment equipment and engineering firms would gain a large new market building the filtration systems [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: People drinking arsenic-tainted tap water, especially in small towns

how_it_helps.text: It would have legally required all drinking water systems to cut arsenic to 10 ppb by October 2003 and 3 ppb by October 2006, replacing a 1942-era standard of 50 ppb [S2] [S3].
It authorized $800 million a year in grants for fiscal years 2002-2006 to help public water systems serving fewer than 10,000 people — 94% of all systems — pay for the upgrades [S2] [S3].
The bill's findings cite EPA data that more than 34 million Americans drink water from systems with average arsenic levels posing unacceptable cancer risks [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Public water systems would pay for treatment to remove arsenic, and those costs eventually flow to ratepayers and local budgets — though the bill's $800 million annual grant program targets the smallest systems, which represent 94% of all systems and would otherwise struggle most [S2] [S3]. Federal taxpayers would fund the grants. Communities where arsenic occurs naturally in groundwater, particularly in the West, would face the biggest bills [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Water systems and ratepayers, offset by federal grants

drawbacks.text: Water systems, especially small ones serving under 10,000 people, would bear real treatment costs; the bill's answer was federal grants of up to $800 million a year, but appropriators would still have to fund them annually [S2] [S3].

Some communities — particularly in the arid West, where arsenic occurs naturally in groundwater at high levels — face the largest per-household costs to meet a 3 ppb limit, and even the bill's grants may not cover the full price of upgrading thousands of small systems [S3].

The 3 ppb target was stricter than what EPA ultimately adopted; regulators and some analysts questioned whether the added health benefit at that level justified the added cost compared with a 10 ppb limit, and the bill would have removed EPA's flexibility to balance that judgment [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is strong: the existing 50 ppb standard dated to 1942, before arsenic was known to cause cancer, and the National Academy of Sciences estimated a one-in-100 lifetime cancer risk at that level — far above the one-in-10,000 risk level EPA normally uses for toxins. The bill also softened the cost side by sending federal grants to small systems rather than making towns shoulder compliance alone. The main honest objection is that the strictest step — 3 ppb — was aggressive; EPA itself had debated whether health benefits at that level justified the cost, particularly for arid western communities where arsenic occurs naturally and treatment is most expensive. The grant money helps, but $800 million a year may not fully cover nationwide upgrades for thousands of small systems. Still, the bill's design — strict standard plus federal money — addressed the cost problem rather than ignoring it, and it never even reached a committee vote where such trade-offs could be weighed.

outcome.mechanism: The House committee it was sent to — and the subcommittee it landed on — never acted on it, so it died quietly when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced March 27, 2001 and referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1] [S5].
Two weeks later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Environment and Hazardous Materials, and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
It never reached the House floor and never received a vote in any form before the Congress ended January 3, 2003 [S1] [S5].

The bill's findings argue the 50 ppb standard was set in 1942, before arsenic was known to cause cancer, and that one in 100 people drinking water at that level over a lifetime would develop cancer [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Water systems — and the communities they serve — avoided any binding move to the stricter 3 ppb standard, and no one had to defend its burial on the House floor: it simply never left subcommittee. The bill's sponsor and its 77 cosponsors got a recorded position but no law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Water systems that avoided a stricter arsenic mandate

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill with 13 original cosponsors.

for.name: 1 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — the only Republican to do so.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Subcommittee on Environment and Hazardous Materials
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 16, 2001 and never held it for consideration; no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded.

against.name: Billy Tauzin
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee to which the bill was referred; no markup or vote on it was ever scheduled.

against.name: Bush administration EPA
against.what_they_did: In March 2001 the agency withdrew the pending Clinton-era rule tightening arsenic to 10 ppb, then reinstated the 10 ppb standard in October 2001 after public backlash — establishing a limit stricter than 50 ppb but far looser than this bill's 3 ppb target.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic: 76 of the 77 cosponsors were House Democrats, with just one Republican, and the bill never advanced out of the Republican-led committee.

industries.industry: Public water systems, especially small municipal systems
industries.note: The bill would have required costly treatment upgrades, but its $800 million-a-year grant program directed federal money to systems serving under 10,000 people — the systems least able to pay. Because it died, these systems avoided the stricter 3 ppb requirement altogether.

industries.industry: Water treatment equipment and engineering firms
industries.note: A nationwide mandate to strip arsenic from drinking water would have created a large market for filtration and treatment technology. With the bill dead, that demand never materialized — and neither did the cleaner water it would have helped deliver.

industries.industry: Household water consumers, especially in small and rural towns
industries.note: Not an industry, but the parties the bill was written for: people drinking water from systems with elevated arsenic. The bill offered them a binding, stricter standard plus federal help to pay for it; its death left them with whatever standard EPA enforced.
